quietus.title: Make it Vast, Make a Show: Remembering Rob
quietus.description: Rob Reindorf was an indefatigable Ghanaian powerhouse, who died recently at the age of 77. Unpublished interview and tribute: Filip Kalinowski. Portrait: Sai Galaxy Sampled by J Dilla and Madlib, reissued by Analog Africa and Soundway, the two legendary loose-up-yourself funk albums by Robert Roy “Rob” Reindorf from Ghana – Rob and Make It Fast, Make It Slow – outlived initially being commercial flops on the cut and thrust highlife-driven musical market of Western Africa of the late 1970s. While Rob moved away from the music industry for several decades, European and American crate diggers started to play and edit the eponymous track from his second album to the extent that the album’s…

quietus.title: Ezra Collective – Here Because of Hope
quietus.description: Ezra Collective Here Because of Hope Their fourth album asks why so much Black music born from pain makes people dance. The band needed the answer for practical reasons Here Because of Hope by Ezra Collective The story behind this record is more specific than the concept suggests. After the Mercury Prize in 2023 and a BRIT Award that followed, Ezra Collective found themselves in an unusual line of work. Audiences were coming to their shows expressly to feel good, which meant walking on stage every night as suppliers of joy. Femi Koleoso has been candid that during some of those gigs things were happening, personally and in the wider world, that were painful. The question he ended up with…

Their first LP since 2022's Most Normal, it…

quietus.description: EXAUDI Pocket Universe Four pieces by Cassandra Miller, Andrew Hamilton, Leo Chadburn and Geoff Hannan under the baton of conductor James Weeks Curation is everywhere nowadays: from art biennales to food menus, everything has abespoke theme, bolstered by snazzy presentation, marketing ploys and influencer campaigns. But what happens when you release music without a thematic lynchpin holding things together? Such is the case of Pocket Universe, the most recent offering from the vocal ensemble EXAUDI and conductor James Weeks, released on NMC Recordings. It comprises four pieces by Cassandra Miller, Andrew Hamilton, Leo Chadburn and Geoff Hannan, commissioned by EXAUDI’s annual EXPOSURE…

A reason to look anew at this well-thumbed tale is the release of an official collection of live audio and video recordings - with unreleased, often brilliant material. It has a canny name: Eternal (Live). The music and video is…

quietus.title: Between Facts and Feeling: The Adam Curtis Party Conference
quietus.description: Tariq Goddard attends the first event of its kind and wonders what (if anything) the many speakers have learned from the auteur it was named for I recall my surprise when I was first asked if I was going to a ‘conference’ by a prominent talking head from a left-wing digital organisation. It was at the height of peak Corbyn and I suppose all manner of improbabilities seemed possible, from power moving from one class to another, to a political little-mark like myself attending an event I would sooner choose food poisoning over. Like a majority of my peers during my formative years, I privileged ‘art’ and self expression over public service and duty, viewing politicians as egotists who lacked…

So when It All Comes Down to This was followed by a pair of archive campaigns, the obvious worry was that the well had run dry and the accountants had moved in. What’s arrived instead is two companion albums that go about their business in completely different ways, tied to two anniversaries: 45 years since...

Especially for this ageing hack, who is always forcibly reminded of his own ongoing meander into disconnected irrelevance when…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Neil Young and the Chrome Hearts :: Second Song
aquariumdrunkard.description: At 80, Neil Young remains gloriously unfinished. Second Song , his latest with the Chrome Hearts, is a weathered, luminous meditation on memory, mortality, love, and the strange passage of time. With shimmering textures, warm harmonies, wandering tempos, and that unmistakably vulnerable voice, Young looks backward without quite letting go of the future. An elegiac, deeply human record from an artist still searching for the song.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Índio da Cuíca :: Zing Zing
aquariumdrunkard.description: At 70, Brazilian percussionist Índio da Cuíca reinvented himself as one of the country’s strangest musical voices. His cuíca—usually a squeaky rhythmic accent—is transformed into a melodic instrument of uncanny virtuosity, set against samba, capoeira, Afro-Brazilian spirituals and warped pop forms. On Zing Zing , that “avant-traditional” vision expands further, as cavaquinho, pandeiro, berimbau and bandolim collide with guitars, synths and samples. Samba music from some parallel universe.

aquariumdrunkard.title: HUG :: HUG
aquariumdrunkard.description: Hug is music for the small hours, when the world comes in and out of focus, a record that drifts through the mind’s open windows, carrying with it the sublime and resonant hush of a world at peace in its own unfolding. As warm and comforting as the name implies, Hug embraces you like an old friend, holding space for the warmth of the past, the uncertainty of the future, and the solace of the blossoming present.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Maddy Prior & June Tabor’s Silly Sisters at 50
aquariumdrunkard.description: Maddy Prior and June Tabor’s Silly Sisters is a magical hinge album, a meeting of two transcendent voices and a jolly band of British folk masters. Recorded in 1976 but somehow outside of time, its ancient songs, close harmonies, and loose, luminous performances summon something older than the British folk revival itself. Fifty years on, it remains a timeless gem hiding in plain sight: raw, sophisticated, mysterious, and still not quite given its due.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Radio Free Aquarium Drunkard :: September 2026
aquariumdrunkard.description: Freeform transmissions from Radio Free Aquarium Drunkard on dublab. Airing every third Sunday of the month, RFAD on dublab features the pairing of Tyler Wilcox’s Doom and Gloom from the Tomb and Chad DePasquale’s New Happy Gathering. This month, Chad kicks it off with a roundup of recent 2026 digs. Tyler follows with an hour of existential daydreams and autumnal instrumentals. Sunday, 4-6pm PT.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Bandcamping :: Autumn 2026
aquariumdrunkard.description: Are things feeling autumnal at long last? Not quite. But maybe this selection of recommended sounds, old and new, can help usher in the cooler, crisper season. Bandcamp Friday only rolls around every couple of months. But remember, you can always add a buck or two to the asking price of any album on the platform and voila — every day is Bandcamp Friday.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Nigeria 80: The Explosive Sound World of 1980s Nigeria
aquariumdrunkard.description: The ’70s didn’t end. They just got more elastic. Strut’s Nigeria 80 catches Nigerian popular music in that beautiful, unruly stretch between Afrobeat’s explosion and whatever came next—juju, funk, highlife, reggae, proto-hip-hop, and plenty of glorious cross-pollination along the way.

aquariumdrunkard.title: The Lagniappe Sessions :: Instrumentals (2016-2026)
aquariumdrunkard.description: Aquarium Drunkard’s Lagniappe Sessions have been rolling along at a steady pace since 2011, bringing together a global lineup of artists to offer up cover versions of a few of their favorite tunes. And some of the most imaginative Lagniappes have been those that deliver purely instrumental pleasures, embracing melody, rhythm and texture. We’ve gathered together a 90-minute sampling of those covers from over the past decade, which range from MPB bliss-outs to Takoma School dreamscapes, from free-funk workouts to orchestral jazz. And beyond!

mubi.description: Tender Loving Care (Mike Leigh, 2026). Courtesy of Joseph Lynn. Midway through the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), Canadian prime minister Mark Carney hosted the Canadian Investment Summit, which had its opening gala at the Art Gallery of Ontario. Bringing together business people from more than 30 countries with the stated aim of accelerating investment in the country which has been beset by trade conflicts with the United States, the event also galvanized a range of community groups with diverse objections to protest the summit, which then brought hundreds of police officers and vehicles to the area just north of the festival center. Meanwhile, just south of that center…

mubi.title: Toronto Dispatch: The War Against Memory
mubi.description: Life of Jorge Luis Borges (Mariano Llinás, 2026). Words mean things, but that meaning is always changing. Sometimes those changes are organic, a gradual movement that is driven by the changing needs of speakers. But sometimes those changes are engineered from above, to serve the needs of those in power. After years of algorithmic censorship, we now see words like “unalive” or “le$bean” replacing their antecedents even in conversation, even if only ironically. (As if to prove the point, the plot of the new film by Denis Côté, Nobody’s Violence , manages to hinge on the issue of assisted suicide without ever uttering the s-word. It’s as if the film anticipates the language that will be…

mubi.title: The Action Scene | “The Raid” at 15
mubi.description: The Action Scene explores the form, history, and visceral power of action cinema through its set pieces. Clockwise from top-left: The Raid (Gareth Evans, 2011), Merantau (Gareth Evans, 2009), The Raid 2 (Gareth Evans, 2014), The Raid (Gareth Evans, 2011). It needs virtually no introduction. Fifteen years after its world premiere in the Midnight Madness section of the 2011 Toronto International Film Festival, The Raid (2011) has so shaped the landscape of contemporary action cinema that it’s birthed its own prepositional descriptor: “like The Raid ” adorns sundry headlines to describe any action film featuring some combination of a single-location setting, gritty atmosphere, barbarous…

mubi.title: Defending the Elusive
mubi.description: Last Year in Marienbad (Alain Resnais, 1961). 1 Although it’s seldom acknowledged, one of the supreme pleasures of movies is the confusion and uncertainty often prompted by the beginning of a story, when we’re not yet fully tuned in to what’s going on. As in our sleeping dreams, a sense of infinite possibility stretches before us. That seemingly limitless vista soon disappoints once it is foreshortened into something real and recognizable, such as a place, an environment, a mood, a character, a theme, a genre, or a plot. Yet without these comfortable anchors, something that resembles prenatal bliss envelops our ignorance, and the fact that we can imagine almost anything makes the start of…

mubi.title: Venice Dispatch: The Garden of Forking Paths
mubi.description: NAZA (Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, 2026). To watch my first film at the 83rd Venice Film Festival, I wore a VR headset. I say “watch” when the more accurate verb would be “experience,” at least going by the fest’s preferred vocabulary for what goes down on Lazzaretto Vecchio, an island a stone’s throw away from the Lido. Once used as a checkpoint for Holy Land pilgrims, and then—after the plague reached the lagoon in 1423—a leper colony, it is, in 2026 AD, now home to the virtual reality sidebar. The architecture has barely changed through the centuries. Dotting the high-ceilinged corridors that used to house the city’s moribund, festival guests can find various booths, each promising…

mubi.title: Survival Tactics: A Locarno Critics Academy Correspondence
mubi.description: Notebook, in partnership with the Locarno Critics Academy, presents a series of critical correspondences in which this year’s participants look back at the Swiss film festival. In this final installment, three critics explore how “tendenko,” a Japanese term that implies isolating to survive a tsunami, resonated across the program. “We live in a state of apocalyptic fetishism,” a radio announcer proclaims in Ann Oren’s Objet A (2026), and the slate of films at Locarno this August did little to dissuade its spectators of this assessment. As has been everywhere observed in recent years, the constant sounding of the alarm has become the 21st century’s room tone, and film festivals are not…

mubi.title: Cut and Spliced: A Locarno Critics Academy Correspondence
mubi.description: Notebook, in partnership with the Locarno Critics Academy, presents a series of critical correspondences in which this year’s participants look back at the Swiss film festival. In this second installment, four critics muse on cinema’s ability to splice disparate fragments together. They touch on ecstatic New York sirens, self-preservation in Iran and Palestine, performances that bear the weight of passing time, and an actress’s descent into two-faced delirium in Rome. We hear in Sans soleil (1983) that “Nothing sorts out memories from ordinary moments. It is only later that they claim remembrance, when they show their scars.” This is how I feel about memories all the time. What lingers in…
